senses: The Eurasian bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula).
The profile of a body of water flowing over an obstruction in a vertical drop.
The ability of a sauce or other relatively thick liquid to coat food, the back of a spoon, etc.
ety: From French nappe. Doublet of map, mop, and nape.

senses: A primitive trap, often set in the hope of swindling a win or draw from a losing position.
ety: From cheap + -o (“person with characteristic”, colloquialising suffix).

senses: A Japanese tool and weapon, possibly derived from the masonry trowel, used as a weapon by ninja or samurai.
ety: From Japanese 苦無 (くない, kunai).

senses: Synonym of polyurethane.
ety: From French uréthane, coined (1833) by Jean Baptiste Dumas. Etymonline proposes an apparent decomposition as urée + éther + -ane.

senses: A plant, Strychnos toxifera, formerly used in arrow poisons in South America due to its D-tubocurarine content.
Other South American plants with similar toxins that were also used in arrow poisons, mostly in the family Menispermaceae.
A substance containing the alkaloid D-tubocurarine, used historically as a muscle relaxant during surgery.
ety: From a Cariban language; compare Kari'na urari, Trió urari, wïrari, Akawaio urari, Pemon urari, Macushi urari, referring to various vines of genus Strychnos.

senses: A white linen or cotton robe worn by religious Ashkenazi Jews on holidays, in the synagogue, or at home when leading the Passover seder.
One who speeds: one who exceeds the maximum legal speed limit.
A machine for drawing and twisting slivers to form rovings, in spinning.
A motorized railroad track crew cart.
A fast worker selected by a company to exemplify the rate of work generally expected; a pacesetter.
A drug that destroys blood platelets.
examples: Discharge drugs included antihypertensives, statins, and antiplatelets (aspirin, aspirin/dipyridamole, clopidogrel, aspirin/clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy, and other antiplatelet agents).

senses: A close friend.
A trusted companion or partner in a criminal organization.
ety: Coined between 1655 and 1665 from Ancient Greek χρόνιος (khrónios, “perennial, long-lasting”); see also chrono- (“time”). Initially Cambridge University slang, in sense of “chum”, as “friend of long standing”, with illegal connotation later. Early spellings included chrony, as in 1665 diary by Samuel Pepys, supporting the Greek origin.

senses: Change of form; transformation.
ety: From Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after”) + Ancient Greek φύσις (phúsis, “growth”), equivalent to meta- + -physis.

senses: The study or cataloging of monsters.
ety: From terato- + -logy, from Ancient Greek τέρας (téras, “monster”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
examples: In this way, this analysis has aimed at expanding gaga feminism by undertaking a critical teratology, that is, of course, the study of monsters
Miranda Francus notes that in the West, the image of the fecund female has often been associated with monstrosity: 'misogyny and teratology have always met in the image of the maternal monster'.

senses: Small articles of jewellery, trinkets, etc.
examples: Is not Howel and James's shop filled with all that human art can invent, or human taste display—bijouterie touched with present sentiment, or radiant with future triumph?
The women cultivate and plant the ground, and after feeding their husbands, expend the surplus products in the beads and baubles which compose their bijouterie.

senses: To form a septation.
ety: From septum + -ate (verb-forming suffix) or back-formation from septation.

senses: To move or vibrate (something) with a buzzing sound.
To make a sibilant buzzing or droning sound.
To cause (something) to make such a sound.
(of a panther) To make a vibrating sound in its throat when contented, much like the domestic cat’s purr.
ety: From Middle English whirren, probably from Old Norse: compare Danish hvirre, virre, Norwegian kvirre, Old Norse hvirfla (“to whirl, spread”).

senses: A shapeshifting monster that feeds on fear.
ety: Variant of boggard, recorded since 18th century. As a monster that feeds on fear, coined by British novelist J. K. Rowling in 1999 in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban.
examples: I pushed open the lid, half-expecting a Boggart to burst out of the trunk, taking the form of my worst nightmare.
The boggart has brought you here because it hopes to feed off you like it has been trying to feed off me.

senses: Regular sushi: a piece of raw fish (or other topping) on top of a small oblong brick of sticky white rice.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 握り (nigiri, “grasping, gripping”, short for 握り寿司 nigirizushi, literally “gripped sushi” from the way the sushi rice is molded in the hand).

senses: Opposite of tap; to return (transitive) a card or piece, or (intransitive) all available cards or pieces, to their original orientation (e.g. at the start of a new turn) to indicate that they are ready to be used again.
ety: From un- + tap. * (to release a flow of): Apparently by confusion of unleash (or similar) and tap.

senses: The practice of treating members of different societal groups in a politically, legally, or economically different manner.
examples: Apartheid was a government-enforced form of separatism in which people received unequal social benefits based on race.

senses: Pre-mixed baking mix, generally consisting of flour, a shortening and a leavening agent (for quickly making fresh biscuits, pancakes, dumplings, etc).
ety: From the brand name Bisquick. Blend of biscuit + quick, because the mix was originally sold as a way of making biscuits in "90 seconds from package to oven".
examples: We were limited in money to purchase supplies, so we took a 100 pound sack of potatoes and several sacks of flour and some bisquick, and of course a case of beer.
Squash can be cut up and frozen but what I do is cut it up, let it dry a little and then grind it up combined with some bisquick and an egg and form patties.
He stopped at the store on the way home and bought two whole chickens, and some bisquick and found a farm stand that had sweet corn.

senses: A traditional dark-brown unrefined sugar made from palm tree sap which is used throughout South and Southeast Asia; (by extension) other types of unrefined sugar.
A small-scale production plant that processes sugar cane to make sugar.
ety: Borrowed from Indo-Portuguese jágara, jagra, from Malayalam ചക്കര (cakkara, “jaggery”) or Tamil சக்கரை (cakkarai), from Sanskrit शर्करा (śarkarā, “candied or ground sugar; (chiefly in the plural) grit, gravel, shingle; gravelly soil; pebble”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorkeh₂ (“boulder; gravel”). Doublet of sugar.

senses: A pepper shaker.
A buttress at one side of the court in the game of fives.
A tower capped by a cupola, looking similar to a giant pepper shaker.
Involuntary labor, especially military service, demanded by some established authority.
An enrolling or registering.
ety: From Middle French conscription, from Latin cōnscriptiō (“levying of troops”).

senses: A person who prepares technical drawings and plans.
A person who prepares drafts.
A person who writes a legislative bill.
examples: It is highly improbable that the drafter of the notice ever visualised the form that heavy vehicles of the future would take, but the comprehensive wording still covers modern types.

senses: The crown or uppermost branches of a tree.
The Japanese technique of inserting a board-like material, a cut-out part of the mother-of-pearl inside the shell, into the carved surface of lacquer or wood.
Having, involving, or relating to multiple variables.
Any of several marine gastropods of the family Ranellidae, which have a pointed spiral shell.
ety: From Triton, who blows such a seashell like a trumpet.

senses: A Jewish liturgical poem.
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew פִּיּוּט (piyút). Doublet of poet.

senses: A person who practices futurology.
A cosmetic product intended to fill uneven areas on the outer edges of the lips after applying lipstick, therefore giving a smooth shape.
A recurring tutti passage in Baroque music for orchestra or chorus.
ety: Italian ritornello, diminutive of ritorno (“return”), from ritornare (“to return”): compare French ritournelle.

senses: One who remembers, recalls from memory.
under a hoof
Someone who, during the Irish famine, supplied food such as soup to Catholics who converted to Protestantism.
A (former) Catholic who converted to Protestantism in order to gain such food.
An advocate of collectivism.
The former currency or money of Lithuania, divided into 100 centai.
A person or animal that whoops.
The whooping crane, Grus americana.
The whooper swan, Cygnus cygnus.
examples: Adult whoopers are white and easy to distinguish from sandhills.

senses: A device used for preparing infusions
A shady valley, a dingle; especially one with steep wooded sides and a stream running through it.
The club rush.
examples: When a stream runs in a deep dell, particularly in clay districts, the steep banks and stream form what are called a “dumble” in Nottinghamshire.
Fine electric activity in sound came from the dumbles below the road, the birds piping one against the other, and water mysteriously plashing, issuing from the lake.
Lambley is famous for its ‘dumbles.’ A dumble being a local name for a shallow dale with a stream.
